Home » CEO Spotlight » At Barbara A. M. Romanow’s Saskatoon Tea Party, a Sled Project for Kids Was Funded in 15 Minutes

At Barbara A. M. Romanow’s Saskatoon Tea Party, a Sled Project for Kids Was Funded in 15 Minutes

Sophie Ireland, PhDCEO SpotlightNovember 24, 2026
Discover more
Economy
Read Economics
Executive leadership training
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:08
Instaread

Fifteen minutes. That is how long it took guests at a Saskatoon tea party to fully fund a children’s project called Sleds for Kids.

Community Life Projects Inc. (CLP) hosted the afternoon on October 22, 2026, at a local tea house, which served a high tea with a selection of teas and small sandwiches. The same afternoon raised $8,200 for a three-and-a-half-year-old boy living with a very rare syndrome. Both results came from people from the community sitting down over tea and hearing about projects they could back.

“It was a fun and beautiful afternoon,” said Barbara A. M. Romanow, CLP’s Global Director. “People from the community came and we discussed projects.”

A pitch that feels like a visit

The format is simple. CLP set out its projects on tables around the room, and the people behind them came to explain their work. Some were partners CLP has funded for years. Guests could back a project on the spot, and because CLP is now a registered charity, donors receive a tax receipt.

Sleds for Kids shows how fast that can work. The kokum at St. Mark School described it to guests as Saskatoon’s UN school, with students from about 60 nations. When she went outside with one of the classes, she found the children sledding on torn sleds that were little better than cardboard. She took the story to Romanow, who agreed to help. During the tea party, a donor called in and funded the whole project.

“Oh, the kids are going to be so happy,” the kokum said when she heard.

The boy behind the $8,200

The boy’s grandmother told his story at the tea party. He is a twin, born two months premature about three and a half years ago. After a series of medical complications, genetic testing found a very rare syndrome caused by a spontaneous mutation rather than an inherited one. She said only about 300 people in the world are known to have it.

The treatments he needs are not offered in Saskatchewan, so the family travels out of province. His feeding tube formula costs $1,400 a month and is not covered. His human growth hormone costs $1,500, and he needs a wheelchair.

“I wasn’t aware as a teacher how much it costs to have a special needs child,” his grandmother said.

The family is raising money for his care and raising awareness at the same time, because they believe other people may have the syndrome without knowing it. His grandmother said she has been in touch with a family in the United States who did not get a diagnosis until their daughter was 10.

“We’re just thankful to Barb for helping us,” she said.

Partners who keep coming back

Several people at the tables run projects CLP has backed for years.

A summer camp that started 30 years ago gives children from Saskatoon’s Pleasant Hill community a week at camp, in a safe place, during the summer holidays when life at home is not always safe. CLP’s support pays for at least 100 children to attend. “I don’t have to worry every summer that I’m going to have enough money to support the camp,” the camp’s organizer told guests.

The Pleasant Hill Community Powwow began in 2003 with a $500 budget, after many years in which powwows were banned. It now draws more than 2,000 people and over 150 dancers, and CLP is one of its main funders. Organizers said one girl who danced there as a tiny tot now teaches powwow dancing. CLP also funds a powwow at Oskayak High School in Saskatoon, which has about 300 Indigenous, Métis, and Inuit students.

Newer projects were on the tables too. A free theatre-in-the-park program for children, which Romanow had already been funding, is now open to public donations. “Now that we’re a charity I’m putting it on the table, because I think this is something that people would love to donate to,” Romanow said. A local salon owner also presented a plan to give 1,000 haircuts inside about 14 inner-city schools, with licensed hairdressers doing the work on site.

“This is community working together,” Romanow said. “I encourage people, please, come and get involved in these things, because it just makes you feel good even to just be involved in these things.”

“We received lots of community support,” Romanow said.

Rooted in Saskatchewan

The event fits where CLP has done most of its work. “We have completed the bulk of our projects in Saskatchewan thus far,” Romanow said.

CLP began its community service work in 2020 as a non-profit and became a registered federal charity on January 29, 2026. Its mission is to create projects in communities that improve the well-being of families and children. A local tea party puts that mission in front of the neighbors it serves.

Once a month, with new projects each time

The October afternoon went well enough that CLP is making it a regular event. “I’m going to have a tea party once a month moving forward. It was a huge success,” Romanow said.

Each tea party will feature new projects, so returning guests always have something fresh to consider and fund. For a charity that funds projects one at a time, a monthly event gives each new project its own audience.

CLP posted a video of the October event on YouTube.
